Evaluation of deep eutectic solvent pretreatment towards efficacy of enzymatic saccharification using multivariate analysis techniques
Salim Massayev, Kiat Moon Lee *
Department of Chemical & Petroleum Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Technology and Built Environment, UCSI University, 56000, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
## ARTICLE INFO --- Handling Editor: M.T. Moreira --- ### Keywords: Lignocellulosic biomass Deep eutectic solvent Pretreatment Multivariate analysis Principal component analysis Partial least square

ABSTRACT In this paper, deep eutectic solvent (DES) pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass was analysed using principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) methods to determine correlations between the pretreatment process variables and assess their significance level. The analysis was conducted on the dataset containing 103 experimental observations and 32 variables. Both PCA and selected PLS model (M4) had substantial prediction power and prediction relevance, as exhibited by their good cumulative explained variance (R2cum, 0.787) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.524) for six principal components of PCA model, and explained variance of independent variable (R2Xcum, 0.781), explained variance of dependent variable (R2Ycum, 0.803) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.776) for the best PLS model. The results of PCA and PLS analyses revealed that the most significant variables for DES pretreatment were severity factor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size, agitation intensity and type of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) of the DES. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. The models also showed that enzymatic saccharification was more efficient when organic solvent or inorganic salt solution was used as antisolvent for lignocellulose regeneration. Usage of water as antisolvent was associated with reduced glucose yield during saccharification. Another notable outcome of this work was that intensive stirring during pretreatment had negative effect on glucose yield due to the shear thickening properties of DESs. This work provided a systematic analysis of DES pretreatment process of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA and PLS methods that allowed better understanding of the factors affecting the pretreatment process.

## 1. Introduction The global trends to waste minimization and reduction of fossil fuel usage stipulated great research interest to alternative energy sources. Lignocellulose is one of the most abundant renewable sources of carbohydrates and therefore it is viewed as a primary candidate for producing biofuels. The major challenge in lignocellulose bioconversion is the high recalcitrance of raw lignocellulosic biomass, that is attributed to the presence of crystalline cellulose regions in the lignocellulose structure (Lee et al., 2021), high resistance of lignin to chemical attacks (Lauberte et al., 2021), as well as the complex polymeric structure of lignocellulose (Lobato-Peralta et al., 2021). Generally, satisfactory efficacy of lignocellulose bioconversion can be achieved only with the aid of a specific pretreatment that could efficiently disrupt lignin-cellulose bonds and reduce the overall crystallinity of cellulose. Conventional

pretreatment methods like acid hydrolysis, pyrolysis, alkaline treat- ment, organic solvent treatment, ozonation, steam explosion, carbon dioxide explosion, and ammonia fiber explosion involve harsh treatment conditions resulting into partial loss of sugars due to degradation (Mahmood et al., 2016). Non-conventional pretreatment methods such as ultrasonic (Lee et al., 2020), ionic liquid (IL) (Lee et al., 2015), and deep eutectic solvent (DES) (Thi and Lee, 2019) are conducted at mild conditions and therefore can boast significantly lesser sugar loss. Within this paper, DES pretreatment was considered. DES pretreatment is a promising method for lignocellulose pretreatment that features superior biocompatibility, low environmental impact, and versatility (Abbott et al., 2004).

DES is a mixture of at least two components one of which is hydrogen bonding acceptor (HBA) and another is hydrogen bonding donor (HBD) whose melting point is significantly lower than that of the individual components and generally not exceeding 100 °C (Abbott et al., 2004).

There are four groups of DESs depending on their HBA and HBD. Type I DESs are composed of organic salts, most frequently a quaternary ammonium salt, and non-hydrated metal halides such as zinc chloride (ZnCl2), iron (III) chloride (FeCl3), copper (II) chloride (CuCl2), lithium chloride (LiCl) and silver chloride (AgCl). Hydrated metal halides are introduced in type II DES. In type III DESs, HBD is represented by a polyalcohol, organic acid, or amide, while HBA remains same the same as type I and type II DESs, i.e. organic salt. While type IV DESs are formed by eutectic mixtures consist of inorganic transition metals with HBD such as urea, ethylene glycol, 1,6-hexanedoil and acetamide. Type III DESs are the most studied type due to easily synthesis, non-reactivity with water, wide range solubility of transition metal, biodegradable and economically feasible (Loow et al., 2017). DES is widely recognized as a green solvent due to its low toxicity, volatility, flammability, and high recyclability (Zdanowicz et al., 2018).

Multiple researchers have reported favorable changes in the struc- ture and composition of lignocellulosic biomass after DES treatment, such as selective removal of hemicellulose and lignin, reduction of cel- lulose crystallinity (Sai and Lee, 2019), and increases in biomass parti- cles surface area (Lee et al., 2021), which lead to enhanced enzymatic saccharification efficiency and productivity. Most of these works were focused on small number of process variables, such as pretreatment temperature, pretreatment duration, biomass-to-solvent ratio, biomass particle size, and Kamlet-Taft parameters of DES. Generally, the authors altered one parameter of pretreatment process at a time and observed how it would affect pretreatment efficiency. Such approach neglects correlations between process variables other than the selected few. Moreover, it is relatively rare for several independent researchers to have identical basis, which makes it troublesome to compare results of current experiment with those conducted by other researchers.

One of the options to resolve these issues is to employ multivariate data analysis that can simultaneously analyze the effect of multiple variables on the pretreatment process efficacy and compare results of large number of research data while considering differences in experi- ments bases (Li et al., 2017). Principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) are two of the most used techniques for multivariate data analysis. PCA is commonly used as a first-look tool to identify relationships between variables that can be further investigated in detail with other techniques (Mahmoudi et al., 2019). It employs latent variables to reduce the dimensionality of the initial dataset and determine the correlation between independent variables. On the other hand, PLS is utilized to evaluate the significance of the relationships between selected dependent and independent variables (Hajilary et al., 2018). It develops a linear regression model by projecting the predicted dependent variable matrix and the observed independent variable ma- trix to a latent variable space. Therefore, both PCA and PLS can be used to estimate the contribution of different variables to the pretreatment efficacy.
In this study, multivariate analysis of DES pretreatment of various

types of lignocellulosic biomass was conducted to fill this knowledge gap. To the best knowledge of the authors, only one multivariate anal- ysis study has been conducted on DES pretreatment of lignocellulose by Xu et al. (2020). However, some of the important pretreatment pa- rameters such as type of antisolvent, stirring rate, and saccharification duration were not considered. In this work, all the important variables in DES pretreatment including pretreatment conditions, type of anti- solvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties were investigated. The main objectives of this work were to investigate the relationships between various parameters of green sol- vent pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA, to study the significance of various parameters of green solvent pretreatment using PLS and to evaluate the quality of the developed PCA and PLS models.

## 2. Methodology ### 2.1. Data collection Dataset on lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment with various DESS was obtained by tabulation of experiment conditions and results published by other researchers in the period from 2004 to present. Different species of lignocellulosic biomass were included in this study. All the data were extracted from various credible online journals and scientific databases such as ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and ACS Publications.

2.2. Multivariate analysis In this work, PCA and PLS analysis of the dataset containing 103 observations and 27 important variables of DES pretreatment was performed with the use of SIMCA 14.1.0.2047 (Soft Independent Modelling of Class Analogy, Umetrics). Variables considered in PCA and PLS were: pretreatment conditions (temperature, pretreatment duration, severity factor, solid-to-liquid loading, biomass particle size and agitation intensity), type of antisolvent (pure water, organic and inorganic solvent (i.e. water with additives)), biomass composition (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin content), general characteristics and type of HBD (number of hydroxyl groups, carboxyl groups, amino groups, and class of chemical compound: polyol, hydroxyl acid, carboxylic acid, or amide), physicochemical properties of DES and HBD (HBD molecular weight, HBD carbon number, HBD melting point, HBD boiling point, HBD pKa, viscosity, DES melting point, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond acidity, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft dipolarity-polarizability), and enzymatic hydrolysis efficacy metrics (saccharification duration and glucose yield). List of variables investigated with their corresponding abbreviations used in the models can be found in Appendix A.

## 2.3. Data preprocessing Both PCA and PLS models cannot work with categorical variables, therefore all categorical variables were replaced with dummy variables. For example, non-binary categorical variable "type of HBD" which can be either polyol, hydroxy acid, amide, or carboxylic acid was replaced with four binary numeric variables, where "1" indicated that certain HBD type was used and "0" indicated the opposite. The variable type for all the investigated variables is presented in Table A1. To maintain consistency, glucose yields that were expressed in terms of weigh of glucose per weigh of biomass were converted to weigh of glucose per weigh of cellulose by dividing glucose yield expressed on the biomass weight basis by cellulose content in the pretreated biomass. Biomass particle sizes that were presented in the form of fraction remaining between two mesh sizes after screening were expressed as the arithmetic average of the maximum and minimum particle size in that fraction.

Every successive principal component account for smaller variance than the previous one. In PCA model M1, six principal components accounted for 78.7% of the total variability of the dataset. From Table 2, cumulative explained variance (R2cum) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum) for six principal components were 0.787 and 0.524, respectively. The value of R2cum represents the proportion of variable for all the original variables. The closer its value to 1, the better the analysis results of the PCA model. As rule of thumb, models with R2cum above 0.75 are said to have substantial predictive power (Eriksson et al., 2013). Q2cum is the measure of the model's prediction relevance. Models with the value of Q2cum above 0.5 and the difference R2cum and Q2cum not exceeding 0.2 to 0.3 are considered to have good predictive relevance (Eriksson et al., 2013). Therefore, the PCA model M1 was sufficiently reliable to explain the DES pretreatment process.

To determine relations between different variables, three loading scatter plots with the highest combined explained variance for a pair of principal components were analyzed. On the loading scatter plot, vari- ables located close to each other within one quadrant are positively correlated, while negatively correlated variables appear in the opposite quadrants relative to the origin. The distance from the point of origin to a certain variable reveals the degree of influence of the variable on the model. The further away a variable located from the origin the more influence it has on the overall model, while the variables located close to the origin point have a low contribution to the model.

Similarly, the severity factor was also positively correlated with glucose yield, which coincided with the conclusion of multiple publications (Lloyd and Wyman, 2005; Nguyen et al., 2000; Scelsi et al., 2021; Schell et al., 2003). PCA analysis is based on linear transformation of original data, therefore it may not be suitable for temperature effect study on glucose yield. Since severity factor is calculated as a logarith- mic function of pretreatment duration and temperature; therefore, ac- cording to the results of PCA model analysis, high severity of treatment with prolonged pretreatment duration and reduced temperature should be used to maximize glucose yield.

Different types of antisolvents had varying effect on glucose yield. Organic and inorganic solution antisolvents had a strong positive correlation with glucose yield, while water antisolvent was correlated to glucose yield in an inverse manner. In other words, organic and inorganic solution based antisolvents were more beneficial to glucose yield rather than deionized water. As for the composition of lignocellulose, glucose yield was inversely related to lignin content. Type of HBD also played a significant role in DES pretreatment efficiency. Hydroxy acid and carboxylic acid DES had a strong positive effect on glucose yield. Polyol based HBD and number of hydroxyl groups were positively correlated with saccharification duration. On the other hand, carboxylic acid and amide based HBD, as well as the number of their characteristic functional groups negatively correlated to saccharification duration. In other words, polyol based HBD were associated with lower lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment efficacy. This could be caused by partial condensation of chemical structures of biomass in polyols (Al Ameri, 2017). As for physiochemical properties of DES, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond basicity had a weak positive influence on glucose yield, while Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond acidity and dipolarity-polarizability had negative correlation. On the other hand, hydrogen bond acidity and dipolarity-polarizability had positive correlation with saccharification duration. Besides, saccharification duration also had a weak positive correlation with pKa of HBD and negative relation with viscosity, HBD melting point, and DES melting point.

According to Doherty et al. (2010), pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass with IL possessing high hydrogen bond basicity resulted in greater glucose and xylose yield. Similar finding were obtained for DES pretreatment (Lee et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2016). These correlates well with the finding of present work. However, correlations of glucose yield

with hydrogen bond acidity contradicted the results of the study con- ducted by Xia et al. (2018). Xia et al. (2018) reported that DESs with higher hydrogen bond acidity shown better efficiency in biomass delignification than DESs with lower hydrogen bond acidity. Thus, hydrogen bond acidity is expected to be positively correlated with glucose yield, while the opposite was shown by the PCA model. A possible cause of this contradiction is the large difference between Kamlet-Taft parameters used by Xia et al. (2018) and in the present study. As shown in Table 3, the difference between the Kamlet-Taft parameter values given by Florindo et al. (2018) and Xia et al. (2018) was quite large. Due to scarcity of publications on Kamlet-Taft param- eters of DESs, it is not possible to determine which researcher provided accurate values, therefore values proposed by Florindo et al. (2018) were used in this study since they also provided Kamlet-Taft parameters for several other DESs.

Positive correlation of particle size with glucose yield was obtained in the PCA model. The positive correlation of particle size with glucose yield agreed with the work conducted by Liu et al. (2013). Nevertheless, different findings were reported by other researchers on the effect of particle size on biomass pretreatment. For instance, Semerci and Ersan (2021) reported that moderate particle size of 0.15–1.18 mm was most effective in enhancing pretreatment performance, compared to smaller or larger particle size of <0.15 mm and >1.18 mm. In another work conducted by Wang et al. (2020), better pretreatment performance was reported with smaller biomass size. These suggested that the increase in surface area with the reduction of particle size may not be the sole reason in influencing the pretreatment performance, but other factors such as mass transfer efficiency and changes in viscosity with reduced particle size should be considered. The combined effect may result in non-linear correlation between particle size and glucose yield. As a result, PCA analysis may not be suitable since it is based on linear

Positive correlation of agitation intensity with the saccharification duration was obtained in the PCA model. It is generally believed that the stirring rate has a positive effect on pretreatment efficacy due to the improvement of mass transfer and reduction of apparent viscosity. However, in the case of non-Newtonian fluids, an increase of shear rate can result in both an increase of apparent viscosity, which is known as a shear thickening, or non-linear decrease of viscosity, which is known as shear thinning. According to Elhamarnah et al. (2019), the majority of DESs are non-Newtonian fluids exhibiting shear thinning behavior. For example, choline chloride:glucose (1:1), choline chloride:citric acid (1:1), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:urea (1:2) exhibit decrease of viscosity with increasing shear rate at room temperature. Only one DES was reported to exhibit shear thickening behavior in that study, which is choline chloride:lactic acid (1:1) at 85 °C. Moreover, the presence of suspended solid particles could change the liquid behavior to non-Newtonian liquids, and in most cases resulted in shear thickening (Brown and Jaeger, 2014). Therefore, it can be hypothesized that the addition of finely milled lignocellulosic biomass to DES might produce a mixture that exhibits shear thickening properties. The viscosity of such fluid would increase at a high stirring rate, which in turn would negatively affect pretreatment efficacy. Further research on rheological behavior of DES with the presence of lignocellulosic biomass should be performed.

Fig. 2 displays R2cum and Q2cum for each variable considered in all principal components of the PCA model. The green bars represent R2cum that describes how well a variable can be explained and the blue bars represent Q2cum that can tell how well a variable can be predicted. In other words, the R2cum is the measure of the contribution of a certain variable to the predictive power of the overall model, while Q2cum is a measure of the variable bias or dependence degree on specific data used for model training. A good model is expected to have high predictive power that does not change with inclusion or exclusion of certain observations from the original dataset (Eriksson et al., 2013). Majority of the variables had high explained variance indicating that they were significant to the model. Solid-to-liquid ratio, cellulose, and lignin content had R2cum slightly below 0.5, which means they had a small contribution to the model comparing to other variables. R2cum was sufficiently high only for half of the variables. Q2cum for particle size, organic antisolvent, inorganic antisolvent, saccharification duration, cellulose content, lignin content, dipole moment, HBD carbon number,

hydroxy acid, carboxylic acid, HBD boiling point, and hydrogen bond acidity were below 0.5, which indicated that these variables could be biased. One variable that stood out among all other was solid-to-liquid ratio; it was the only variable with negative Q2cum, which meant it had no predictive relevance.

One of the possible causes of low R2cum and Q2cum is experimental data bias. Since the training dataset for this analysis was obtained by the tabulation of conditions and results of experiments performed by other researchers, the obtained data might be biased due to the unreported differences in the treatment and measurement procedures. For example, values of hydrogen bond acidity of choline chloride:glycerol with a molar ratio of 1:2 measured by different researchers were 1.49 (Florindo et al., 2018), 0.32 (Degam, 2017), and 1.18 (Xia et al., 2018), as shown in Table 3. The second reason for low explained and predicted variance is the non-linearity of relations between some of the variables. PCA model calculation is based on the linear approximation of data (Eriksson et al., 2013). If two variables are related non-linearly, the linear approximation will lead to the loss of some portion of data resulting in a less accuracy of the model.

3.2. Partial least square analysis of DES pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass PLS is a mathematical optimization technology that determines the best fit function by minimizing the square error. PLS input is a dataset with assigned dependency relations among the variables. The major motivation to use PLS is to verify hypothesized relations between independent and dependent variables. In this study, four different PLS models were studied by including different combinations of independent variables. PLS model M2 focused on effect of pretreatment conditions. PLS model M2 provides a reference for evaluating the effect of inclusion of other variable groups into a different PLS model. For example, antisolvents were included in PLS model M3, while type of antisolvent and biomass composition were considered in PLS model M4. PLS model M5 considered all the above-mentioned variable groups with the inclusion of type of HBD in DES and its physicochemical properties.

4. Conclusion With both PCA and PLS multivariate analysis methods, the rela- tionship between the pretreatment condition, type of antisolvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties on glucose yield and saccharification duration were analyzed. PCA model for DES pretreatment included six principal components that accounted for 78.8% of the total variability and had a cumulative predicted vari- ance of 0.524, which indicated its good predictive power and relevance. This model suggested that glucose yield could be improved by longer pretreatment duration at a lower temperature but with a large resulting severity factor. The model showed that organic and inorganic anti- solvents are more beneficial for glucose yield rather than water anti- solvent. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. Glucose yield in this model was favored by larger size particles. Unex- pectedly, intensive agitation tended to increase the time required to complete enzymatic saccharification. This could be potentially explained by the non-Newtonian properties of DES, and the formation of shear-thickening fluid upon mixing DES with fine lignocellulose parti- cles. PLS model M4 was selected as the best model to describe the effect of various DES pretreatment parameters on saccharification efficacy

evaluation parameters. R2Xcum, R2Ycum, and Q2cum of the model were 0.781, 0.803, and 0.776, indicating its substantial prediction power for dependent variables and prediction relevance. The most sig- nificant variables affecting the pretreatment process were severity fac- tor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size and agitation intensity. The correlations obtained in this work could play a significant role in guiding the researchers in selecting appropriate pretreatment variables in optimizing the DES pretreatment.

Moreira --- ### Keywords: Lignocellulosic biomass Deep eutectic solvent Pretreatment Multivariate analysis Principal component analysis Partial least square ABSTRACT In this paper, deep eutectic solvent (DES) pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass was analysed using principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) methods to determine correlations between the pretreatment process variables and assess their significance level. The analysis was conducted on the dataset containing 103 experimental observations and 32 variables. Both PCA and selected PLS model (M4) had substantial prediction power and prediction relevance, as exhibited by their good cumulative explained variance (R2cum, 0.787) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.524) for six principal components of PCA model, and explained variance of independent variable (R2Xcum, 0.781), explained variance of dependent variable (R2Ycum, 0.803) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.776) for the best PLS model. The results of PCA and PLS analyses revealed that the most significant variables for DES pretreatment were severity factor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size, agitation intensity and type of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) of the DES. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. The models also showed that enzymatic saccharification was more efficient when organic solvent or inorganic salt solution was used as antisolvent for lignocellulose regeneration. Usage of water as antisolvent was associated with reduced glucose yield during saccharification. Another notable outcome of this work was that intensive stirring during pretreatment had negative effect on glucose yield due to the shear thickening properties of DESs. This work provided a systematic analysis of DES pretreatment process of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA and PLS methods that allowed better understanding of the factors affecting the pretreatment process. ## 1. Introduction The global trends to waste minimization and reduction of fossil fuel usage stipulated great research interest to alternative energy sources. Lignocellulose is one of the most abundant renewable sources of carbohydrates and therefore it is viewed as a primary candidate for producing biofuels. The major challenge in lignocellulose bioconversion is the high recalcitrance of raw lignocellulosic biomass, that is attributed to the presence of crystalline cellulose regions in the lignocellulose structure (Lee et al., 2021), high resistance of lignin to chemical attacks (Lauberte et al., 2021), as well as the complex polymeric structure of lignocellulose (Lobato-Peralta et al., 2021). Generally, satisfactory efficacy of lignocellulose bioconversion can be achieved only with the aid of a specific pretreatment that could efficiently disrupt lignin-cellulose bonds and reduce the overall crystallinity of cellulose. Conventional pretreatment methods like acid hydrolysis, pyrolysis, alkaline treat- ment, organic solvent treatment, ozonation, steam explosion, carbon dioxide explosion, and ammonia fiber explosion involve harsh treatment conditions resulting into partial loss of sugars due to degradation (Mahmood et al., 2016). Non-conventional pretreatment methods such as ultrasonic (Lee et al., 2020), ionic liquid (IL) (Lee et al., 2015), and deep eutectic solvent (DES) (Thi and Lee, 2019) are conducted at mild conditions and therefore can boast significantly lesser sugar loss. Within this paper, DES pretreatment was considered. DES pretreatment is a promising method for lignocellulose pretreatment that features superior biocompatibility, low environmental impact, and versatility (Abbott et al., 2004). DES is a mixture of at least two components one of which is hydrogen bonding acceptor (HBA) and another is hydrogen bonding donor (HBD) whose melting point is significantly lower than that of the individual components and generally not exceeding 100 °C (Abbott et al., 2004). * Corresponding author. Type I DESs are composed of organic salts, most frequently a quaternary ammonium salt, and non-hydrated metal halides such as zinc chloride (ZnCl2), iron (III) chloride (FeCl3), copper (II) chloride (CuCl2), lithium chloride (LiCl) and silver chloride (AgCl). Hydrated metal halides are introduced in type II DES. In type III DESs, HBD is represented by a polyalcohol, organic acid, or amide, while HBA remains same the same as type I and type II DESs, i.e. organic salt. While type IV DESs are formed by eutectic mixtures consist of inorganic transition metals with HBD such as urea, ethylene glycol, 1,6-hexanedoil and acetamide. Type III DESs are the most studied type due to easily synthesis, non-reactivity with water, wide range solubility of transition metal, biodegradable and economically feasible (Loow et al., 2017). DES is widely recognized as a green solvent due to its low toxicity, volatility, flammability, and high recyclability (Zdanowicz et al., 2018). Multiple researchers have reported favorable changes in the struc- ture and composition of lignocellulosic biomass after DES treatment, such as selective removal of hemicellulose and lignin, reduction of cel- lulose crystallinity (Sai and Lee, 2019), and increases in biomass parti- cles surface area (Lee et al., 2021), which lead to enhanced enzymatic saccharification efficiency and productivity. Most of these works were focused on small number of process variables, such as pretreatment temperature, pretreatment duration, biomass-to-solvent ratio, biomass particle size, and Kamlet-Taft parameters of DES. Generally, the authors altered one parameter of pretreatment process at a time and observed how it would affect pretreatment efficiency. Such approach neglects correlations between process variables other than the selected few. Moreover, it is relatively rare for several independent researchers to have identical basis, which makes it troublesome to compare results of current experiment with those conducted by other researchers. One of the options to resolve these issues is to employ multivariate data analysis that can simultaneously analyze the effect of multiple variables on the pretreatment process efficacy and compare results of large number of research data while considering differences in experi- ments bases (Li et al., 2017). Principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) are two of the most used techniques for multivariate data analysis. PCA is commonly used as a first-look tool to identify relationships between variables that can be further investigated in detail with other techniques (Mahmoudi et al., 2019). It employs latent variables to reduce the dimensionality of the initial dataset and determine the correlation between independent variables. On the other hand, PLS is utilized to evaluate the significance of the relationships between selected dependent and independent variables (Hajilary et al., 2018). It develops a linear regression model by projecting the predicted dependent variable matrix and the observed independent variable ma- trix to a latent variable space. Therefore, both PCA and PLS can be used to estimate the contribution of different variables to the pretreatment efficacy. In this study, multivariate analysis of DES pretreatment of various types of lignocellulosic biomass was conducted to fill this knowledge gap. To the best knowledge of the authors, only one multivariate anal- ysis study has been conducted on DES pretreatment of lignocellulose by Xu et al. (2020). However, some of the important pretreatment pa- rameters such as type of antisolvent, stirring rate, and saccharification duration were not considered. In this work, all the important variables in DES pretreatment including pretreatment conditions, type of anti- solvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties were investigated. The main objectives of this work were to investigate the relationships between various parameters of green sol- vent pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA, to study the significance of various parameters of green solvent pretreatment using PLS and to evaluate the quality of the developed PCA and PLS models. ## 2. Methodology ### 2.1. Data collection Dataset on lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment with various DESS was obtained by tabulation of experiment conditions and results published by other researchers in the period from 2004 to present. Different species of lignocellulosic biomass were included in this study. All the data were extracted from various credible online journals and scientific databases such as ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and ACS Publications. 2.2. Multivariate analysis In this work, PCA and PLS analysis of the dataset containing 103 observations and 27 important variables of DES pretreatment was performed with the use of SIMCA 14.1.0.2047 (Soft Independent Modelling of Class Analogy, Umetrics). Variables considered in PCA and PLS were: pretreatment conditions (temperature, pretreatment duration, severity factor, solid-to-liquid loading, biomass particle size and agitation intensity), type of antisolvent (pure water, organic and inorganic solvent (i.e. water with additives)), biomass composition (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin content), general characteristics and type of HBD (number of hydroxyl groups, carboxyl groups, amino groups, and class of chemical compound: polyol, hydroxyl acid, carboxylic acid, or amide), physicochemical properties of DES and HBD (HBD molecular weight, HBD carbon number, HBD melting point, HBD boiling point, HBD pKa, viscosity, DES melting point, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond acidity, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft dipolarity-polarizability), and enzymatic hydrolysis efficacy metrics (saccharification duration and glucose yield). List of variables investigated with their corresponding abbreviations used in the models can be found in Appendix A. 2 S. Massayev and K.M. Lee Journal of Cleaner Production 360 (2022) 132239 ## 2.3. Data preprocessing Both PCA and PLS models cannot work with categorical variables, therefore all categorical variables were replaced with dummy variables. For example, non-binary categorical variable "type of HBD" which can be either polyol, hydroxy acid, amide, or carboxylic acid was replaced with four binary numeric variables, where "1" indicated that certain HBD type was used and "0" indicated the opposite. The variable type for all the investigated variables is presented in Table A1. To maintain consistency, glucose yields that were expressed in terms of weigh of glucose per weigh of biomass were converted to weigh of glucose per weigh of cellulose by dividing glucose yield expressed on the biomass weight basis by cellulose content in the pretreated biomass. Biomass particle sizes that were presented in the form of fraction remaining between two mesh sizes after screening were expressed as the arithmetic average of the maximum and minimum particle size in that fraction. ### 3. Results and discussion In this work, the effect of different DES pretreatment conditions on the efficiency of lignocellulose enzymatic hydrolysis was investigated using multivariate data analysis with PCA and PLS methods. Variables considered in PCA and PLS are shown in Table 1. 3.1. *Principal component analysis of DES pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass* PCA works through dimensional reduction of large data set by transforming a large set of variables into a smaller data set with most of the information retains. The first principal component (p[1]) was calculated such that it accounts for the greatest possible variance in the dataset. Every successive principal component account for smaller variance than the previous one. In PCA model M1, six principal components accounted for 78.7% of the total variability of the dataset. From Table 2, cumulative explained variance (R2cum) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum) for six principal components were 0.787 and 0.524, respectively. The value of R2cum represents the proportion of variable for all the original variables. The closer its value to 1, the better the analysis results of the PCA model. As rule of thumb, models with R2cum above 0.75 are said to have substantial predictive power (Eriksson et al., 2013). Q2cum is the measure of the model's prediction relevance. Models with the value of Q2cum above 0.5 and the difference R2cum and Q2cum not exceeding 0.2 to 0.3 are considered to have good predictive relevance (Eriksson et al., 2013). Therefore, the PCA model M1 was sufficiently reliable to explain the DES pretreatment process. To determine relations between different variables, three loading scatter plots with the highest combined explained variance for a pair of principal components were analyzed. On the loading scatter plot, vari- ables located close to each other within one quadrant are positively correlated, while negatively correlated variables appear in the opposite quadrants relative to the origin. The distance from the point of origin to a certain variable reveals the degree of influence of the variable on the model. The further away a variable located from the origin the more influence it has on the overall model, while the variables located close to the origin point have a low contribution to the model. More research on effect of particle size on pretreat- ment performance should therefore be performed. Positive correlation of agitation intensity with the saccharification duration was obtained in the PCA model. It is generally believed that the stirring rate has a positive effect on pretreatment efficacy due to the improvement of mass transfer and reduction of apparent viscosity. However, in the case of non-Newtonian fluids, an increase of shear rate can result in both an increase of apparent viscosity, which is known as a shear thickening, or non-linear decrease of viscosity, which is known as shear thinning. According to Elhamarnah et al. (2019), the majority of DESs are non-Newtonian fluids exhibiting shear thinning behavior. For example, choline chloride:glucose (1:1), choline chloride:citric acid (1:1), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:urea (1:2) exhibit decrease of viscosity with increasing shear rate at room temperature. Only one DES was reported to exhibit shear thickening behavior in that study, which is choline chloride:lactic acid (1:1) at 85 °C. Moreover, the presence of suspended solid particles could change the liquid behavior to non-Newtonian liquids, and in most cases resulted in shear thickening (Brown and Jaeger, 2014). Therefore, it can be hypothesized that the addition of finely milled lignocellulosic biomass to DES might produce a mixture that exhibits shear thickening properties. The viscosity of such fluid would increase at a high stirring rate, which in turn would negatively affect pretreatment efficacy. Further research on rheological behavior of DES with the presence of lignocellulosic biomass should be performed. Fig. 2 displays R2cum and Q2cum for each variable considered in all principal components of the PCA model. The green bars represent R2cum that describes how well a variable can be explained and the blue bars represent Q2cum that can tell how well a variable can be predicted. In other words, the R2cum is the measure of the contribution of a certain variable to the predictive power of the overall model, while Q2cum is a measure of the variable bias or dependence degree on specific data used for model training. A good model is expected to have high predictive power that does not change with inclusion or exclusion of certain observations from the original dataset (Eriksson et al., 2013). Majority of the variables had high explained variance indicating that they were significant to the model. Solid-to-liquid ratio, cellulose, and lignin content had R2cum slightly below 0.5, which means they had a small contribution to the model comparing to other variables. R2cum was sufficiently high only for half of the variables. Q2cum for particle size, organic antisolvent, inorganic antisolvent, saccharification duration, cellulose content, lignin content, dipole moment, HBD carbon number, hydroxy acid, carboxylic acid, HBD boiling point, and hydrogen bond acidity were below 0.5, which indicated that these variables could be biased. One variable that stood out among all other was solid-to-liquid ratio; it was the only variable with negative Q2cum, which meant it had no predictive relevance. One of the possible causes of low R2cum and Q2cum is experimental data bias. Since the training dataset for this analysis was obtained by the tabulation of conditions and results of experiments performed by other researchers, the obtained data might be biased due to the unreported differences in the treatment and measurement procedures. For example, values of hydrogen bond acidity of choline chloride:glycerol with a molar ratio of 1:2 measured by different researchers were 1.49 (Florindo et al., 2018), 0.32 (Degam, 2017), and 1.18 (Xia et al., 2018), as shown in Table 3. The second reason for low explained and predicted variance is the non-linearity of relations between some of the variables. PCA model calculation is based on the linear approximation of data (Eriksson et al., 2013). If two variables are related non-linearly, the linear approximation will lead to the loss of some portion of data resulting in a less accuracy of the model. 3.2. Partial least square analysis of DES pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass PLS is a mathematical optimization technology that determines the best fit function by minimizing the square error. PLS input is a dataset with assigned dependency relations among the variables. The major motivation to use PLS is to verify hypothesized relations between independent and dependent variables. In this study, four different PLS models were studied by including different combinations of independent variables. PLS model M2 focused on effect of pretreatment conditions. PLS model M2 provides a reference for evaluating the effect of inclusion of other variable groups into a different PLS model. For example, antisolvents were included in PLS model M3, while type of antisolvent and biomass composition were considered in PLS model M4. Conclusion With both PCA and PLS multivariate analysis methods, the rela- tionship between the pretreatment condition, type of antisolvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties on glucose yield and saccharification duration were analyzed. PCA model for DES pretreatment included six principal components that accounted for 78.8% of the total variability and had a cumulative predicted vari- ance of 0.524, which indicated its good predictive power and relevance. This model suggested that glucose yield could be improved by longer pretreatment duration at a lower temperature but with a large resulting severity factor. The model showed that organic and inorganic anti- solvents are more beneficial for glucose yield rather than water anti- solvent. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. Glucose yield in this model was favored by larger size particles. Unex- pectedly, intensive agitation tended to increase the time required to complete enzymatic saccharification. This could be potentially explained by the non-Newtonian properties of DES, and the formation of shear-thickening fluid upon mixing DES with fine lignocellulose parti- cles. PLS model M4 was selected as the best model to describe the effect of various DES pretreatment parameters on saccharification efficacy evaluation parameters. R2Xcum, R2Ycum, and Q2cum of the model were 0.781, 0.803, and 0.776, indicating its substantial prediction power for dependent variables and prediction relevance. The most sig- nificant variables affecting the pretreatment process were severity fac- tor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size and agitation intensity. The correlations obtained in this work could play a significant role in guiding the researchers in selecting appropriate pretreatment variables in optimizing the DES pretreatment. Moreira --- ### Keywords: Lignocellulosic biomass Deep eutectic solvent Pretreatment Multivariate analysis Principal component analysis Partial least square ABSTRACT In this paper, deep eutectic solvent (DES) pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass was analysed using principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) methods to determine correlations between the pretreatment process variables and assess their significance level. The analysis was conducted on the dataset containing 103 experimental observations and 32 variables. Both PCA and selected PLS model (M4) had substantial prediction power and prediction relevance, as exhibited by their good cumulative explained variance (R2cum, 0.787) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.524) for six principal components of PCA model, and explained variance of independent variable (R2Xcum, 0.781), explained variance of dependent variable (R2Ycum, 0.803) and cumulative predicted variance (Q2cum, 0.776) for the best PLS model. The results of PCA and PLS analyses revealed that the most significant variables for DES pretreatment were severity factor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size, agitation intensity and type of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) of the DES. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. The models also showed that enzymatic saccharification was more efficient when organic solvent or inorganic salt solution was used as antisolvent for lignocellulose regeneration. Usage of water as antisolvent was associated with reduced glucose yield during saccharification. Another notable outcome of this work was that intensive stirring during pretreatment had negative effect on glucose yield due to the shear thickening properties of DESs. This work provided a systematic analysis of DES pretreatment process of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA and PLS methods that allowed better understanding of the factors affecting the pretreatment process. ## 1. Introduction The global trends to waste minimization and reduction of fossil fuel usage stipulated great research interest to alternative energy sources. Lignocellulose is one of the most abundant renewable sources of carbohydrates and therefore it is viewed as a primary candidate for producing biofuels. The major challenge in lignocellulose bioconversion is the high recalcitrance of raw lignocellulosic biomass, that is attributed to the presence of crystalline cellulose regions in the lignocellulose structure (Lee et al., 2021), high resistance of lignin to chemical attacks (Lauberte et al., 2021), as well as the complex polymeric structure of lignocellulose (Lobato-Peralta et al., 2021). Generally, satisfactory efficacy of lignocellulose bioconversion can be achieved only with the aid of a specific pretreatment that could efficiently disrupt lignin-cellulose bonds and reduce the overall crystallinity of cellulose. Conventional pretreatment methods like acid hydrolysis, pyrolysis, alkaline treat- ment, organic solvent treatment, ozonation, steam explosion, carbon dioxide explosion, and ammonia fiber explosion involve harsh treatment conditions resulting into partial loss of sugars due to degradation (Mahmood et al., 2016). Non-conventional pretreatment methods such as ultrasonic (Lee et al., 2020), ionic liquid (IL) (Lee et al., 2015), and deep eutectic solvent (DES) (Thi and Lee, 2019) are conducted at mild conditions and therefore can boast significantly lesser sugar loss. Within this paper, DES pretreatment was considered. DES pretreatment is a promising method for lignocellulose pretreatment that features superior biocompatibility, low environmental impact, and versatility (Abbott et al., 2004). DES is a mixture of at least two components one of which is hydrogen bonding acceptor (HBA) and another is hydrogen bonding donor (HBD) whose melting point is significantly lower than that of the individual components and generally not exceeding 100 °C (Abbott et al., 2004). * Corresponding author. Type I DESs are composed of organic salts, most frequently a quaternary ammonium salt, and non-hydrated metal halides such as zinc chloride (ZnCl2), iron (III) chloride (FeCl3), copper (II) chloride (CuCl2), lithium chloride (LiCl) and silver chloride (AgCl). Type III DESs are the most studied type due to easily synthesis, non-reactivity with water, wide range solubility of transition metal, biodegradable and economically feasible (Loow et al., 2017). DES is widely recognized as a green solvent due to its low toxicity, volatility, flammability, and high recyclability (Zdanowicz et al., 2018). Multiple researchers have reported favorable changes in the struc- ture and composition of lignocellulosic biomass after DES treatment, such as selective removal of hemicellulose and lignin, reduction of cel- lulose crystallinity (Sai and Lee, 2019), and increases in biomass parti- cles surface area (Lee et al., 2021), which lead to enhanced enzymatic saccharification efficiency and productivity. Most of these works were focused on small number of process variables, such as pretreatment temperature, pretreatment duration, biomass-to-solvent ratio, biomass particle size, and Kamlet-Taft parameters of DES. Generally, the authors altered one parameter of pretreatment process at a time and observed how it would affect pretreatment efficiency. Such approach neglects correlations between process variables other than the selected few. Moreover, it is relatively rare for several independent researchers to have identical basis, which makes it troublesome to compare results of current experiment with those conducted by other researchers. One of the options to resolve these issues is to employ multivariate data analysis that can simultaneously analyze the effect of multiple variables on the pretreatment process efficacy and compare results of large number of research data while considering differences in experi- ments bases (Li et al., 2017). Principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least square (PLS) are two of the most used techniques for multivariate data analysis. PCA is commonly used as a first-look tool to identify relationships between variables that can be further investigated in detail with other techniques (Mahmoudi et al., 2019). It employs latent variables to reduce the dimensionality of the initial dataset and determine the correlation between independent variables. On the other hand, PLS is utilized to evaluate the significance of the relationships between selected dependent and independent variables (Hajilary et al., 2018). It develops a linear regression model by projecting the predicted dependent variable matrix and the observed independent variable ma- trix to a latent variable space. Therefore, both PCA and PLS can be used to estimate the contribution of different variables to the pretreatment efficacy. In this study, multivariate analysis of DES pretreatment of various types of lignocellulosic biomass was conducted to fill this knowledge gap. To the best knowledge of the authors, only one multivariate anal- ysis study has been conducted on DES pretreatment of lignocellulose by Xu et al. (2020). However, some of the important pretreatment pa- rameters such as type of antisolvent, stirring rate, and saccharification duration were not considered. In this work, all the important variables in DES pretreatment including pretreatment conditions, type of anti- solvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties were investigated. The main objectives of this work were to investigate the relationships between various parameters of green sol- vent pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass using PCA, to study the significance of various parameters of green solvent pretreatment using PLS and to evaluate the quality of the developed PCA and PLS models. ## 2. Methodology ### 2.1. Data collection Dataset on lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment with various DESS was obtained by tabulation of experiment conditions and results published by other researchers in the period from 2004 to present. Different species of lignocellulosic biomass were included in this study. All the data were extracted from various credible online journals and scientific databases such as ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and ACS Publications. 2.2. Multivariate analysis In this work, PCA and PLS analysis of the dataset containing 103 observations and 27 important variables of DES pretreatment was performed with the use of SIMCA 14.1.0.2047 (Soft Independent Modelling of Class Analogy, Umetrics). Variables considered in PCA and PLS were: pretreatment conditions (temperature, pretreatment duration, severity factor, solid-to-liquid loading, biomass particle size and agitation intensity), type of antisolvent (pure water, organic and inorganic solvent (i.e. water with additives)), biomass composition (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin content), general characteristics and type of HBD (number of hydroxyl groups, carboxyl groups, amino groups, and class of chemical compound: polyol, hydroxyl acid, carboxylic acid, or amide), physicochemical properties of DES and HBD (HBD molecular weight, HBD carbon number, HBD melting point, HBD boiling point, HBD pKa, viscosity, DES melting point, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond acidity, Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft dipolarity-polarizability), and enzymatic hydrolysis efficacy metrics (saccharification duration and glucose yield). Positive correlation of agitation intensity with the saccharification duration was obtained in the PCA model. It is generally believed that the stirring rate has a positive effect on pretreatment efficacy due to the improvement of mass transfer and reduction of apparent viscosity. However, in the case of non-Newtonian fluids, an increase of shear rate can result in both an increase of apparent viscosity, which is known as a shear thickening, or non-linear decrease of viscosity, which is known as shear thinning. According to Elhamarnah et al. (2019), the majority of DESs are non-Newtonian fluids exhibiting shear thinning behavior. For example, choline chloride:glucose (1:1), choline chloride:citric acid (1:1), choline chloride:glycerol (1:2), and choline chloride:urea (1:2) exhibit decrease of viscosity with increasing shear rate at room temperature. Only one DES was reported to exhibit shear thickening behavior in that study, which is choline chloride:lactic acid (1:1) at 85 °C. Moreover, the presence of suspended solid particles could change the liquid behavior to non-Newtonian liquids, and in most cases resulted in shear thickening (Brown and Jaeger, 2014). Therefore, it can be hypothesized that the addition of finely milled lignocellulosic biomass to DES might produce a mixture that exhibits shear thickening properties. The viscosity of such fluid would increase at a high stirring rate, which in turn would negatively affect pretreatment efficacy. Further research on rheological behavior of DES with the presence of lignocellulosic biomass should be performed. Conclusion With both PCA and PLS multivariate analysis methods, the rela- tionship between the pretreatment condition, type of antisolvent, biomass composition, type of DES and its physicochemical properties on glucose yield and saccharification duration were analyzed. PCA model for DES pretreatment included six principal components that accounted for 78.8% of the total variability and had a cumulative predicted vari- ance of 0.524, which indicated its good predictive power and relevance. This model suggested that glucose yield could be improved by longer pretreatment duration at a lower temperature but with a large resulting severity factor. The model showed that organic and inorganic anti- solvents are more beneficial for glucose yield rather than water anti- solvent. The use of carboxylic acid and hydroxy acid HBD was associated with higher glucose yield and shorter duration of saccharification. Glucose yield in this model was favored by larger size particles. Unex- pectedly, intensive agitation tended to increase the time required to complete enzymatic saccharification. This could be potentially explained by the non-Newtonian properties of DES, and the formation of shear-thickening fluid upon mixing DES with fine lignocellulose parti- cles. PLS model M4 was selected as the best model to describe the effect of various DES pretreatment parameters on saccharification efficacy evaluation parameters. R2Xcum, R2Ycum, and Q2cum of the model were 0.781, 0.803, and 0.776, indicating its substantial prediction power for dependent variables and prediction relevance. The most sig- nificant variables affecting the pretreatment process were severity fac- tor, temperature, type of antisolvent, particle size and agitation intensity. The correlations obtained in this work could play a significant role in guiding the researchers in selecting appropriate pretreatment variables in optimizing the DES pretreatment.
